It wants the same treatment as the Triumphs: a timed sequence you can stand in. |

### Chapter IV  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 30–46

*Research: **enumerated**. Had ZERO features and its own block said nobody had enumerated it. Read from the naming of the four wonders through the proportion figure, the digression on the architect, the right-hand stylobate and the forge relief cut on it, to the point where he goes in at the porch. Adds 8. Three of them are the chapter's plates, left at `unknown` rather than `unbuilt` because they have not been read against the world yet, which is the recipe's rule. The largest find is that this chapter is mostly ARCHITECTURAL THEORY -- the porch is the occasion for the book to state its own rule of proportion and its own picture of the architect -- and the world carries none of it.*  
*Text: Dallington 1592 — `C:\Dev\hypnerotomachia polyphili\md\Hypnerotomachia_by_Francesco_Colonna.md`*  
*Tour: The Great Portal (portal, 12 notes)*

All four are built. What is wrong is that they are not one set on the ground: the horse, colossus and elephant stand past the portal while the book has them in the court before it. See ticket bug-piazza-wrong-side-of-portal, which this line is the clearest evidence for -- the four are a single company in a single place.* | place | — | Dallington 1592 p. 55 |
| ○ | The construction of the porch's proportion, drawn on the ground<br>*Poliphilo works out the architect's rule by drawing it: he takes a square off the two columns either side, makes a tetragon ABCD, divides it with three lines each way into sixteen quadrats, adds half as much again to get twenty-four, draws the two diagonals and two more lines to make four quadrats mutually intersecting, then sets four median points in the void over the isopleures and joins them into a rhombus. This is the book being a treatise for a page, and it is the reason the porch is described at all. Nothing in the world shows it; grepping for tetragon, rhombus and quadrat finds only unrelated canvas code.* | inscription | — | Dallington 1592 p. 55 |
| ○ | What the architect must be, and the rule of the solid<br>*The digression the proportion figure sets off. Take away order and rule and nothing can be made beautiful or durable; ornament may be added or diminished, but the SOLID -- the body of the frame, its invention and symmetry -- must be kept whole. Then the architect himself: honest, no prattler, courteous, patient, full of new devices, a curious searcher into all arts, and not subject to avarice. Belongs in the commentary layer rather than in geometry, but it is one of the few places the book states its own method, and the world does not carry it anywhere.* | inscription | — | Dallington 1592 pp. 56-57 |

Before him a winged goddess holding her naked infant on her thighs, her foot set on a stone by a furnace sunk in a hollow, her hair dressed high -- and the smiths at their work cannot stop looking at her. _reliefTexture now dispatches to a named scene first and falls back to the seeded crowd only where the book merely gestures at a relief. The register is carved silhouette -- each shape drawn twice, dark below and light above, which is how every relief in this world is made. It is not fine drawing and does not try to be. Cost: nothing. ### Chapter XI  · Book 1 · 1499 pp. 141–146

*Research: **enumerated**. Chapter XI has NO PLATE of its own and, until this pass, no feature list -- and it looked covered, which is why it stayed unread. The reason it looked covered is a mistake in tours.json: the Human Chess Match and Logistica and Thelemia were both tagged chapter XI, so this chapter's row showed two tour stops. Both are chapter X. The chess ballet is at 1499 p. 119 -- "Through the way of the curtains there entered thirty-two young girls, of whom sixteen were clothed in cloth of gold" -- and page_119.md's own heading says Chapter X. Retagged in this pass; ticket bug-chapter-xi-tour-misattributed has the consequences.

What the chapter actually contains is one of the hinges of Book I: the bath nymphs leave Poliphilo alone and kindled on a plain, he walks to the end of a flowery covering, an ample plain opens with a countless crowd of youth of BOTH KINDS keeping high festival, and out of that company a nymph comes to him with a BURNING TORCH in her hand. He suspects she is Polia and the strange dress and place talk him out of it. Then five pages of blazon -- gown, girdle, pearls, necklace stone by stone, wreath, hair, eyes -- and a closing quarrel between his eyes and his appetite.

Eleven features. The one that matters is xi-nymph-with-the-torch, and it is PARTIAL for an interesting reason: the world already builds a Polia holding a burning torch, and constants.js already describes her pose as "in the green arbour, before he has recognised her" -- which is this chapter's moment, word for word. She is simply sited three chapters later, in the jasmine arbour, with no festival behind her.*  
*Text: Dallington 1592 — `C:\Dev\hypnerotomachia polyphili\md\Hypnerotomachia_by_Francesco_Colonna.md`*

The abandonment is the point and it is composed, like the spacious plain of chapter I: a place defined by who has just gone out of it. | ✅ | The three doors hewn in the living rock<br>*Built and verified on the running page 2026-09-09 at main.js?v=361, standing at the station (0, 21) looking north to the gates at z = 12.

The note this replaces described a build that no longer exists: "a free-standing 29 m masonry wall on a garden axis, the wrong ground, the wrong material and the wrong mood". The wall with its entablature and Corinthian columns — the opposite of "as plaine as might be" — had already been replaced by rock: a bank of boulders rising behind and above the gates, a straight-cut rock face with the three openings hewn from it, rough reveals, and the green moss the book gives the right-hand gate's leaves. So the material and the mood were right and the ledger had simply not been told.

What was still wrong was the GROUND, which is the third of the three faults and the one the book is most insistent about: "without any greene grasse or hearbe". The meadow was excluded from a strip only 2.8 m deep at the foot of the rock, so grass grew over the whole approach a reader actually crosses, and the stony ground stopped short of it. Now the exclusion covers the seat (x -15.5..15.5, z 5.5..19.5), the stone apron runs back to z = 19 to meet it, and 54 broken stones are strewn across it for "full of broken and nybled stones" — small, flat and un-collided, since the book's complaint is that the place is harsh underfoot, not that it is hard to cross.

Cost, measured: 5 621 -> 5 625 meshes and 3 101 652 -> 3 103 586 triangles. The 54 stones merge to about four draws because they share a material.

Still short of the book in one respect, recorded rather than hidden: the crags rise "as high as a man might looke to" and ours are a bank of boulders a few metres tall. The mountains behind are not built.* | building | `world/portal.js _buildDoorsWall; the meadow exclusion in world/nature.js` | Dallington p. 192 |
